63-001.r: Viruses → replicate only inside living cells and can infect all life forms: animals, plants, bacteria and fungi (1, 2 and 3).

63-002.r: Citrus canker → bacterium Xanthomonas (lesions on leaves, stems, fruit; early drop); red rot of sugarcane → fungus. The book gives no single answer (*).

63-003.r: Paddy → brown leaf spot; Wheat → black rust; Sugarcane → red rot; Pigeon pea (arhar) → wilt (ukhtha rog).

63-004.r: Wrong pair: Sugarcane – powdery mildew (that affects wheat, grape, barley, onion, apple, pea). Correct: wheat–Phalaris minor, potato–late blight, bajra–ergot.

63-005.r: Wrong pair: Rice – green hair; green hair is a bajra disease (twisted, broom-like heads, dwarf plants). Correct: bajra–ergot, pea–powdery mildew, gram–wilt.

63-006.r: Wrong pair: Paddy – wilt; wilt affects gram, chickpea, sugarcane, toor. Correct: mustard–white rust, bajra–smut, groundnut–tikka.

63-007.r: Nitrogen deficiency → yellowing (uniform chlorosis, older leaves first) and stunted growth; nitrogen needed for chlorophyll and protein.

63-008.r: Zinc (Zn, micronutrient) deficiency → chlorosis in maize; white tips on maize leaves, dwarf plants.

63-010.r: Zinc deficiency → white bud of maize; also khaira of rice, mottle leaf (little leaf) or frenching of citrus and cotton.

63-011.r: Pyrilla → leafhopper pest of sugarcane; sucks leaf sap, causing yellow patches and drying of leaves.

63-012.r: Tikka → deadly disease of groundnut: early and late leaf spot by fungi Cercospora personata and Cercospora arachidicola.

63-013.r: White rust → fungal disease of mustard, caused by Albugo candida (white patches on stem, leaves, inflorescence).
63-013.t: White rust = mustard; black rust = wheat.

63-014.r: Rice blast → fungal disease (Pyricularia oryzae / Magnaporthe oryzae), one of the most destructive rice diseases.

63-015.r: False statement: false smut in barley; false smut is a paddy disease (chalky grains). Correct: rust–wheat, early blight–potato, khaira–paddy.

63-016.r: Two common fungal diseases of wheat → black rust (Puccinia graminis tritici) and loose smut (Ustilago nuda tritici).
63-016.t: White rust is of mustard, not wheat.

63-017.r: Karnal bunt → fungal disease of wheat by smut fungus Tilletia indica; first reported 1931 near Karnal, Haryana.
63-017.h: Karnal (Haryana) is wheat country → Karnal bunt of wheat.

63-018.r: Rice tungro → two viruses (RTSV spherical, RTBV bacilliform) transmitted together by green leafhoppers.

63-019.r: Plant diseases spread by birds, dust, rain and wind (all four); also animals, soil, seed, pollen, irrigation water, humans.

63-020.r: Blackheart of potato → abiotic disease from oxygen deficiency during storage.

63-021.r: Yellow vein mosaic → viral disease of okra (bhindi), spread by whitefly.

63-023.r: Spongy tissue (soft white corky centre, ripening disorder) → Alphonso mango; hampers its export; peculiar to South India.

64-001.r: Microsatellite DNA → short DNA segments repeated many times at one spot; used as markers to study evolutionary relationships among fauna species.

64-002.r: NOT possible: functional chromosomes from DNA of different species. Possible: artificial functional DNA, DNA replicating outside a cell, cells dividing in petri dishes.

64-003.r: Insulin → first human hormone made by recombinant DNA technology; Humulin (Eli Lilly, Genentech bacteria) approved by US FDA in 1982.

64-004.r: Recombinant vector vaccines → made by genetic engineering; live weakened bacteria or viruses used as vectors to carry antigen genes. Both statements true.

64-005.r: Recombinant DNA technology → genes can move across plant species, from animals to plants, and from microorganisms to higher organisms (all).

64-006.r: Making rDNA: isolate genetic material → fragment DNA → isolate desired fragment → amplify gene → ligate into vector → transfer to host → get product → downstream processing.

64-007.r: DNA can be cut and pasted at will (A true) using restriction endonucleases (cut) and DNA ligases (join) (R explains A); Nobel 1978: Arber, Nathans, Smith.

64-008.r: Ligases → molecular stitchers (join DNA by covalent bonds); restriction endonucleases → molecular scissors.
64-008.t: Scissors cut = restriction endonuclease; stitcher joins = ligase.

64-009.r: Personalised (precision) medicine → CRISPR, nanotechnology, robotics and 3D bioprinting all play a role. The book gives no single answer (*).

64-010.r: Cas9 (CRISPR associated protein 9) → molecular scissors that cut DNA in targeted gene editing; CRISPR = clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats.

64-011.r: RNA interference (RNAi) → silences genes by neutralising mRNA; used for gene silencing therapies, cancer therapies, virus-resistant crops (1, 2, 4), not hormone replacement.

64-012.r: Messenger RNA (mRNA) → single-stranded ribonucleic acid; carries genetic code from DNA in nucleus to ribosomes for protein making; basis of mRNA vaccines.

64-013.r: Pronuclear transfer → 'three-parent baby' IVF technique to prevent mitochondrial diseases in offspring (faulty mitochondria removed).

64-014.r: Mitochondrial replacement therapy (mitochondrial donation) can prevent passing mitochondrial disease, before or after IVF (1 true); book marks 'entirely from mother' (2) incorrect.

64-015.r: Dolly → first mammal cloned from an adult somatic cell (A true), by cloning, not in vitro fertilisation (R false); Roslin Institute, Scotland, 1996.

64-016.r: Dolly the sheep → born 5 July 1996 (not 1998) in Scotland; died 14 February 2003 of lung disease; first cloned mammal from adult somatic cell.
64-016.h: Dolly lived 1996–2003: died months before her seventh birthday.

64-020.r: NDRI Karnal → world's first cloned buffalo calf Samrupa (hand-guided cloning, February 2009); second clone Garima (June 2009, 43 kg).

64-021.r: Garima II → cloned buffalo by NDRI Karnal (22 Aug 2010); gave birth to calf Mahima on 25 January 2013.

64-022.r: Ganga → India's first cloned Gir cow (female calf), NDRI Karnal, born 16 March 2023, 32 kg.

64-023.r: Taiwan → first transgenic glowing green pigs (National Taiwan University, 2006), by putting glowing green protein in pig embryos.

64-024.r: Injaz → world's first cloned camel (female), Camel Reproduction Centre, Dubai, UAE.

64-025.r: Clone → produced asexually; genetically identical to its parent; two clones are identical; identical twins are not clones (book).

64-026.r: Test-tube baby (IVF) → fertilisation outside the mother's body (in a petri dish); embryo then implanted in the uterus.

64-027.r: Genetic engineering successes: disease resistance, growth promotion, animal cloning (1, 2, 3); human cloning not achieved (controversial, banned).
